explanation: Sisters Mildred and Patty Hill published it as 'Good Morning to All', a song for teachers and pupils to start the day. Birthday words were later sung to the same melody.

claims.text: The melody of Happy Birthday to You was published in 1893 as Good Morning to All, a morning greeting song for kindergarten children.
Mildred Hill and Patty Hill, who were sisters, published Good Morning to All.
The birthday lyrics were later sung to the melody of Good Morning to All.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for 'false': most players assume the birthday song was written as one; the 1893 kindergarten songbook printed the tune as Good Morning to All, so the statement is true. Similar earlier tunes exist, which is why the statement says 'was published' rather than 'was written'. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: the song is sung in many languages worldwide. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: c1 is dated and needs a source. I left out the long copyright dispute.

evidence.restatement: The Happy Birthday tune first appeared in print in 1893 as Good Morning to All, a greeting song for kindergarten classes.
